original.text:
Except murder, and offences against the State punishable with
death, nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is compelled to
do it by threats, which, at the time of doing it, reasonably cause the
apprehension that instant death to that person will otherwise be the
consequence:
Provided that the person doing the act did not of his own accord, or
from a reasonable apprehension of harm to himself short of instant death,
place himself in the situation by which he became subject to such
constraint.
Explanation 1.—A person who, of his own accord, or by reason of a
threat of being beaten, joins a gang of dacoits, knowing their character, is
not entitled to the benefit of this exception, on the ground of his having
been compelled by his associates to do anything that is an offence by law.
Explanation 2.—A person seized by a gang of dacoits, and forced, by
threat of instant death, to do a thing which is an offence by law; for
example, a smith compelled to take his tools and to force the door of a
house for the dacoits to enter and plunder it, is entitled to the benefit of
this exception.
Act causing slight harm.

original.chapter_title: OF FALSE EVIDENCE AND OFFENCES AGAINST PUBLIC JUSTICE
original.text: Whoever, knowing or having reason to believe that any persons are about to commit or have recently committed robbery or dacoity, harbours them or any of them, with the intention of facilitating the commission of such robbery or dacoity, or of screening them or any of them from punishment, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
original.derived_context:

Chapter 14: OF FALSE EVIDENCE AND OFFENCES AGAINST PUBLIC JUSTICE
Section 254: Penalty for harbouring robbers or dacoits.
Whoever, knowing or having reason to believe that any persons are about to commit or have recently committed robbery or dacoity, harbours them or any of them, with the intention of facilitating the commission of such robbery or dacoity, or of screening them or any of them from punishment, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

phase11.final_answer: Section 32 provides that a person compelled by threats causing reasonable apprehension of instant death is not committing an offence, except for murder and certain state offences, provided they did not voluntarily place themselves in that situation.
phase11.summary_answer: Section 32 states that a person compelled by threats that cause reasonable apprehension of instant death is not committing an offence, except for murder and certain state offences.
phase11.detailed_answer: According to Section 32 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, a person who is compelled to act by threats that reasonably cause the apprehension of instant death is not committing an offence, with the exception of murder and offences against the State punishable by death. However, this provision does not apply if the person voluntarily placed themselves in a situation where they could be subjected to such threats. For instance, a person who joins a gang of dacoits knowing their character cannot claim this exception, while a person forced by a gang under threat of instant death to commit an offence may be entitled to this exception.

llm_evidence.text: Except murder, and offences against the State punishable with death, nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is compelled to do it by threats, which, at the time of doing it, reasonably cause the apprehension that instant death to that person will otherwise be the consequence: Provided that the person doing the act did not of his own accord, or from a reasonable apprehension of harm to himself short of instant death, place himself in the situation by which he became subject to such constraint. Explanation 1.—A person who, of his own accord, or by reason of a threat of being beaten, joins a gang of dacoits, knowing their character, is not entitled to the benefit of this exception, on the ground of his having been compelled by his associates to do anything that is an offence by law. Explanation 2.—A person seized by a gang of dacoits, and forced, by threat of instant death, to do a thing which is an offence by law; for example, a smith compelled to take his tools and to force the door of a house for the dacoits to enter and plunder it, is entitled to the benefit of this exception.
